n: This declaration was adopted by a Church general assembly in Kirtland on August 17, 1835, and included in the first edition of the Doctrine and Covenants. It is a statement of belief, not a revelation. It begins: governments are ordained by God for people’s good, and God holds lawmakers and officials accountable.

f.g: The section was likely written by Oliver Cowdery while Joseph Smith was away; it reflects the Church’s official position.

n: Peaceful government must protect three things: freedom of conscience, the right to own and control property, and the protection of life.
Governments need officials to enforce laws. People should seek out and support fair, just officials—by vote in a republic or by the ruler’s choice in a monarchy.
Religion comes from God, and people answer to God alone for how they worship—unless their practices infringe on others’ rights. Government should restrain crime but never control conscience.

f.w: should restrain crime, but never control conscience

n: Citizens should support the governments that protect their rights; rebellion against such governments is wrong. Governments may make laws for the public good while respecting freedom of conscience.

f.g: Speech or action inciting rebellion against the government.
Unable to be taken away or given up.

n: Leaders deserve honor for protecting the innocent and punishing the guilty. Without laws, anarchy follows. Human laws govern relations among people; divine laws govern faith and worship. We answer to God for both.
Governments must protect religious freedom and have no right to punish people for their beliefs, provided they respect the law and do not promote rebellion.
Crimes should be punished according to their seriousness by the laws where they occur, and all citizens should help bring lawbreakers to justice.
Religion and civil government should not be mixed so that one church is favored and another oppressed.

f.w: mingle religious influence with civil government
f.g: The Saints had felt the effects of religious hostility in Missouri.

n: Churches may discipline their own members regarding fellowship, but may not seize property, threaten life, or inflict physical punishment. The most a church can do is excommunicate.
Wrongs should be taken to the courts. But people may defend themselves, their friends, property, and government from unlawful attack in an emergency when the law can’t help in time.

f.g: Remedy or compensation for a wrong.

n: Written in 1835 after Missourians accused the Saints of stirring up enslaved people, this verse states the Church would not preach to or baptize enslaved people against their masters’ will. It reflects that era’s legal and political pressures. Later scripture and teaching affirm that God invites all to come unto him, “black and white, bond and free.”
